judgement.summary: A seven-chapter scroll built on one through-line question ("What does it take before a number is trusted enough to act on?") and one object — eight abstracted extruded city blocks, one per employer or project, that rearrange into a tenure timeline, a toolchain stack, a project grid and a final lit whole, with the live Lisbon Rent Map as the only checkable proof. Its greatest weakness is that it carries the source material's inflated descriptions straight onto the page as caption copy ("real-time fraud detection system", "automation platform for analytics teams", "Supported sequencing operations", "genomic runs"), so the to-confirm markers sit beside claims the plan has already asserted; secondarily, the seven chapters map almost one-to-one onto About/Experience/Skills/Projects/Testimonials/Contact under field-flavoured names.

traps.evidence: "I take you to be a dashboard-and-data person who's moved from genomics into banking" — no question about what he actually did at Helix.
"The genomics paper — were you an author, and what did you contribute?"
"Helix reporting-time reduction: your resume says 40%, the export says 60%."
"FraudShield — built where, for whom...? Ever in production? Anyone else on it with you?"
"AutoPilot — built at Meridian or independently? Anyone else using it? Is it something you can actually show...?"
"The Meridian '35% efficiency' figure — what does it measure, over what period, and is it your result or the dashboard/team's?"
"can I name Helix Genomics / Meridian Bank at all, including any screenshots of dashboards built there?"; "Is there anything that must not be shown?"
"Lisbon Rent Map traffic: resume says 5,000 visitors/month, export says 3,000/month"; "monthly average or a peak?"
"MSc Data Science end date: resume says 2021, export says 2022."
"Health Data Hackathon 2023 — what did the winning project do, was it a team, and what was your part?"
"DataTugas — what is it: a company, a student group, a side project? What did you yourself do there?"

invented.claim: That the data he works with is "genomic runs, bank transactions, or rent listings" — implying he modelled genomic and bank transaction data; nothing in the material says what tables he worked from, and he never touched the science at Helix.
invented.where: Third reply, Chapter 4 "The Model"; docs/story/storyboard.md beat 4.1

invented.claim: That SQL/Python → dbt/Statistics → Tableau/Power BI is "your actual toolchain, literally" — the material gives an unordered skills list, not a pipeline he uses.
invented.where: Second reply; third reply Chapter 4; docs/story/storyboard.md beat 4.1

final.question: What does it take before a number is trusted enough to act on?
final.form: The shipping ritual behind a public data product: The Question → The Analyst → The Data → The Model → The Map → The Readers → The Next Release
final.object: Eight simple extruded blocks — abstracted, explicitly not-to-scale city blocks — one per employer and project

swap.reason: The object and the climax are justified by the one public thing only he built — the Lisbon Rent Map — and the blocks carry his specific employers, projects and tenure lengths.

backdrop.reason: The arrangements encode real information (block height = tenure in months, layer order = toolchain, grid = project set, accent light = the one checkable project), so deleting the 3D loses structure, not just decoration.

depth.reason: A question is posed on unlit ground, the same eight pieces are progressively ordered, stacked and resolved, and the close answers the opening question — the order cannot be shuffled.

clipart.reason: An abstracted city-block model is not the stock data-analyst emblem, though the tenure-height timeline in Chapter 3 comes close to being a bar chart.

honesty.reason: Page copy still prints "real-time fraud detection system", "automation platform for analytics teams", "Supported sequencing operations" and "genomic runs" as fact, all of which overstate what he did.

thirty_seconds.reason: Screen one gives name and role, and a side rail offers "Proof" (the live rent map) and "Contact" shortcuts that work as plain links everywhere.

plain_reader.reason: "What does it take before a number is trusted enough to act on?" is plain English to an outsider and a real working question to an analyst.
